Blinded cross-architecture replication and the retraction of a super-linear estimate

Paper II of the ARC Theory: the measurement programme of Law I, the ARC Principle, a law under test

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

Paper II of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics: the measurement programme of Law I, the ARC Principle, a law under test, with a blinded cross-architecture replication of the ARC Equation’s exponent and the retraction of a super-linear estimate. It bears in two ways, neither a test, on Law V, the ARC Embedding Law (added on 24 September 2026 and registered as a law on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103 of the theory registration, not yet tested; its mathematics in development), and its Section 7 states, as conditional theorems, the argument behind the Eden Protocol, which criterion F5 would test and which is untested. Working paper, version 2.18, 21 October 2026; first published 22 January 2026; Appendix B gives this version’s corrections and every version note since version 2.10. Recorded on OSF as Paper II · The ARC Theory · Law I, the ARC Principle · Blinded Cross-Architecture Replication and the Retraction of a Super-Linear Estimate, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/8FJMA. Abstract

How much more capable does AI become when it thinks longer? If capability compounded super-linearly with reasoning depth, a safeguard that did not grow with it would fall behind, so the answer bears directly on AI safety. Law I of the ARC Theory, the ARC Principle, a law under test, states that error falls as a power of recursive depth, E(R)=E0R−αE(R)=E_0R^{-\alpha}, and first predicted super-linear suppression (α>1\alpha>1) for sequential reasoning and sub-linear suppression for parallel sampling. We measured α\alpha on competition mathematics in two phases. On DeepSeek R1 with visible reasoning tokens (12 problems), the parallel exponent was α≈0\alpha\approx0, and the sequential endpoint estimate, α≈2.24\alpha\approx2.24 (quadratic), is retracted: it did not replicate in a blinded study across frontier models (18 AIME and Putnam-level problems, n=54n=54 per depth per model, bootstrap intervals, and four-layer cross-verification in which no model checks its own answers). Two models were at or near ceiling, one switched from 54 to 100 per cent as a step and one stayed near 50 per cent; only Gemini 3 Flash scaled smoothly, with regression estimate 0.490.49 (standard error 0.200.20, r2=0.86r^2=0.86, three depth levels) and endpoint estimate 0.590.59, whose bootstrap 95 per cent interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9] contains both zero and two. That is one model’s fit and inconclusive, and its closeness to a reference exponent of one half identifies no mechanism. More samples left the parallel exponent near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, gave 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), and gave none for Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100 per cent; sequential exceeded parallel wherever both exponents could be estimated. Alignment, measured in a companion arm, did not move with capability (one run, under a code-review caveat). We state what would refute the surviving claim and what a deciding measurement requires.

Version 2.18 sets the paper in this form, corrects its statements of the parallel exponents and of Grok 4.1 Fast’s accuracy, records that the answer key of one tier-1 problem was wrong, and states Laws IV and V as registered on 15 October 2026; Appendix B gives each correction and every version note since version 2.10, with its date.

1 Introduction

How much more capable does AI become when it thinks longer? Reasoning models now spend computation at inference time, and the question is not idle: if capability compounded super-linearly with reasoning depth, any safeguard that did not itself grow with depth would fall further behind at every step (Section 7). Whether the returns compound or diminish is a measurement. Law I of the ARC Theory, the ARC Principle, states the form that measurement takes, an error rate falling as a power of recursive depth; it is a law under test, and this paper reports the measurements of its exponent made so far.

The scaling laws governing artificial intelligence have transformed our understanding of capability emergence. Kaplan et al. (2020) established power-law relationships between model performance and training compute, while Hoffmann et al. (2022) refined these with compute-optimal prescriptions. These foundational works revolutionised training methodology but address only pre-training scaling. They do not explain why allocating additional computation at inference time produces dramatic capability improvements, nor why different forms of such computation yield fundamentally different outcomes.

The emergence of reasoning models in late 2024 introduced test-time compute as a critical variable. OpenAI’s o1 (September 2024; OpenAI 2024) and DeepSeek’s R1 (January 2025; DeepSeek-AI 2025a) allocate computational resources during inference to reason before responding. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, these systems achieve performance previously thought to require order-of-magnitude larger models. Yet the mechanisms underlying this improvement remain incompletely characterised.

Two paradigms have emerged for allocating test-time compute:

Parallel recursion.

Generate multiple independent solutions and select the best via majority voting or verifier scoring. This approach is computationally straightforward but, as documented by Brown et al. (2024), produces diminishing returns: coverage grows roughly log-linearly with the number of samples, and majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples.

Sequential recursion.

Generate extended reasoning chains where each step builds explicitly on previous steps. Errors can be detected and corrected iteratively through self-reference. This approach was predicted to produce compounding returns. Earlier work compared sequential and parallel test-time computation and found the direction contested (Section 2); none of the works cited there estimates a separate scaling exponent of error for each form, which this paper measures.

Does sequential reasoning outperform parallel sampling, and does it do so at equal computational cost? If it does, what mathematical principle governs the difference? And what are the implications for aligning increasingly capable AI systems?

The result in plain words. The first measurement, on one model and twelve problems, suggested compounding returns, with an exponent of about 2.24 that is now retracted: a blinded replication across frontier models did not reproduce it. On the harder problems used for the replication, two models were at or near ceiling, one stayed near 50 per cent whatever the depth, and one jumped from 54 to 100 per cent as soon as reasoning was switched on, so only one model gave an exponent that can be fitted at all; that fit’s point estimates are sub-linear and its interval is too wide to decide anything (Section 5.5). Adding independent samples helped little or not at all in four models and clearly in one (Groq Qwen3, from 53.3 to 71.1 per cent over all 30 problems, the model whose depth arm showed no trend), and the sequential exponent was above the parallel one wherever both could be estimated.

Our contributions are as follows.

  1. A two-phase measurement of the depth exponent α\alpha of the ARC Principle, E(R)=E0R−αE(R)=E_0R^{-\alpha} (Definition 1), on competition mathematics: a single-model study on DeepSeek R1, with recursive depth measured directly from visible reasoning tokens (Sections 4.2 and 5.1 to 5.3), and a replication across frontier models with bootstrap intervals and four-layer cross-verification in which no model verifies its own answers (Sections 4.3 and 5.5). Comparisons of the two forms at matched compute came first (Snell et al. 2024; Sharma and Chopra 2025); they report which form wins and by how much rather than a separate exponent for each condition (Section 2).

  2. The retraction of the single-model estimate α≈2.24\alpha\approx2.24, which did not replicate across architectures, with the reasons for its inflation: twelve problems, one model and a compressed dynamic range (Sections 6.2 and 12.5).

  3. The surviving estimates, each with the estimator it belongs to: on Gemini 3 Flash, the one model in the measurable range, a regression estimate of 0.490.49 (standard error 0.200.20, r2=0.86r^2=0.86, three depth levels) and an endpoint estimate of 0.590.59 with bootstrap 95% interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9], one model’s fit and inconclusive; a parallel exponent near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4 and 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash, a majority-vote gain in Groq Qwen3 (from 53.3% to 71.1% over all 30 problems) and none measurable on Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100%; and the sequential exponent above the parallel one wherever both could be estimated (Sections 5.5 and 6).

  4. A classification of what made the exponent uninterpretable in the other four models, ceiling, step function and floor, and of the problem calibration a deciding measurement needs (Sections 5.5 and 11).

  5. The integration with the alignment arm of the same experiment, reported in Paper IV.a: capability and alignment did not move together with depth, which undermines the second condition of the paper’s conditional alignment theorems; that run stands under an October 2026 code-review caveat (Sections 7 and 12.6).

  6. A comparison with quantum error correction, biological scaling laws and consciousness research, each read as an analogy and not as validation (Section 8).

  7. Falsification conditions with their present status, and the two untested assumptions about the sequential and parallel arms on which the contrast rests (Sections 9 and 11.2).

Section 2 places the work among related work. Section 3 states the ARC Principle and the exponent measured, Section 4 the two experimental designs, Section 5 the results of both phases and Section 6 the evidence consolidated across sources. 2 Related work

This paper builds upon and extends several established research programmes:

Chain-of-thought prompting.

Wei et al. (2022) demonstrated that intermediate reasoning steps improve performance on multi-step tasks.

Test-time compute scaling.

Snell et al. (2024) found that, in a FLOPs-matched evaluation, test-time computation can let a smaller model outperform a 14×\times larger one on problems where the smaller model attains a somewhat non-trivial success rate. Setting a chain of revisions against equally many parallel attempts, they found that “sampling solutions in sequence outperforms sampling them in parallel” (narrowly, in their Figure 6), with an ideal ratio of the two on harder questions (their Section 6.1).

Repeated sampling.

Large Language Monkeys (Brown et al. 2024) found that coverage, the fraction of problems solved by any generated sample, scales with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude, often log-linearly, in a relationship that can be modelled with an exponentiated power law.

Self-consistency.

The parallel arm here is majority voting over independent samples, the self-consistency method of Wang et al. (2022), which samples diverse reasoning paths and selects the most consistent answer.

Sequential against parallel, before and after.

Muennighoff et al. (2025), lengthening a single chain by budget forcing, report that “sequential scaling is more effective than parallel” (their Section 4.2, with majority voting run on the base model before fine-tuning); Wu et al. (2025) report that broader initial reasoning “can achieve comparable or superior performance” to deep iterative reasoning; and later work by Gu et al. (2026) reports that “parallel sampling seems to outperform sequential sampling”. The direction is contested, and none of these works estimates a separate exponent for depth and for breadth, the quantity measured here. Recursive depth as a scaling dimension is also prior: Alabdulmohsin and Zhai (2025) introduced Recursive Inference Scaling, “a particular form of recursive depth”, compared in a compute-matched regime.

Self-correction.

Huang et al. (2023) report that large language models “struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback”, which bears on the premise of Section 3.2 that errors are corrected iteratively within a chain.

Reasoning by reinforcement learning.

DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI 2025a) demonstrated reasoning that emerged through pure reinforcement learning in DeepSeek-R1-Zero, with an “aha moment” in an intermediate version of that model, in which it re-evaluated its initial approach; this paper reads that as recursive self-correction.

Concurrent work at matched compute.

Sharma and Chopra (2025) report in ‘The Sequential Edge’ (arXiv:2511.02309, 4 November 2025) that sequential scaling, in which chains explicitly build on previous attempts, beat parallel self-consistency in 95.6% of the configurations they tested, with accuracy gains of up to 46.7% across three reasoning benchmarks; their own token-budget scaling analysis reports that “both paradigms follow similar scaling curves”, with sequential reasoning higher in absolute performance (their Section 6.2, on one benchmark and one model). Their sequential condition refines whole chains, where this paper’s lengthens one. Their paper is dated earlier than the runs recorded here. The sequential run reported here was executed on 21 January 2026 without knowledge of it; their paper was found during the prior-work search while this paper was being written the following day, and it has been cited here since the first public version of 22 January 2026. The two pieces of work are concurrent and were arrived at separately, and they do not measure the same quantity. Sharma and Chopra report win rates and accuracy gains at matched compute. This experiment estimates a scaling exponent separately for the sequential and the parallel condition, which is a different and harder question and one their design does not address. Neither result establishes the other. Reaching the same direction without contact is neither derivation nor corroboration, as the theory registration states, and neither result establishes a scaling law. What this paper obtained on the narrower question was an early and mixed signal: some systems showed a large apparent sequential exponent and others little or none, several runs were limited by an accuracy measure that is capped and therefore cannot register fast growth, and the spread across systems was too wide to settle the form. The strong version of the claim is recorded below as not confirmed. The claim registered for prospective test, proposition P1 of the theory registration (registered 8 September 2026), is accordingly the narrower and harder one: that usable capability is best described by a power law in modelled recursive depth, and that the depth exponent exceeds the compute-matched and token-matched breadth exponent by the margin registered with the deciding instrument.

This paper extends these observations by stating a unified mathematical framework, the ARC Principle, and testing it experimentally, with direct measurement of recursive depth.

Two further concessions stand where their subjects are treated: the d/(d+1)d/(d+1) form of biological scaling is prior work, credited in Section 8.2, and the conjectured quadratic limit is drawn by analogy to Grover’s search bound, whose optimality Bennett et al. (1997) proved (Section 3.4).

3 Theoretical framework

3.1 The ARC Principle

The principle, first articulated in Infinite Architects (manuscript of 8 December 2024; first edition 2026, Eastwood 2026b) and formalised in Paper I (Eastwood, 17 January 2026), predicts that the form of recursion determines the scaling regime: sequential recursion should yield super-linear error suppression (scaling exponent α>1\alpha > 1), while parallel recursion should yield sub-linear suppression (α<1\alpha < 1).

Definition 1 (The ARC Principle). The ARC Principle (Artificial Recursive Creation), Law I of the ARC Theory and a law under test, states that error rates in intelligent systems decrease according to a power law with recursive depth: E(R)=E0×R−α.\begin{equation*} E(R) = E_0 \times R^{-\alpha}. \end{equation*}(1)

In Paper I, Law I’s equation, the ARC Equation, is written for capability as U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}; equation (1) writes the law for the error rate, with the exponent α\alpha.

Table 1. Variable definitions.
Symbol Name Definition Units
E(R)E(R) Error rate at depth RR Proportion of incorrect responses [0,1][0, 1]
E0E_0 Baseline error rate Error rate at minimal recursion (R=1R = 1) [0,1][0, 1]
RR Recursive depth Self-referential processing iterations Tokens or samples
α\alpha Scaling exponent Rate of error suppression Dimensionless

The scaling exponent α\alpha determines the nature of returns from recursive investment:

  • α<1\alpha < 1: Sub-linear suppression. Each doubling of RR reduces error by less than half, and the suppression factor E0/E(R)=RαE_0/E(R) = R^{\alpha} grows more slowly than RR.

  • α=1\alpha = 1: Linear suppression. Each doubling of RR halves error, and the suppression factor grows in proportion to RR.

  • α>1\alpha > 1: Super-linear suppression. Each doubling of RR more than halves error, and the suppression factor grows faster than RR.

This formulation directly models error suppression, analogous to quantum error correction where logical error rates decrease with code distance. The exponent α\alpha encapsulates the efficiency of the recursive process.

3.2 Two fundamentally different forms of recursion

We distinguish two architecturally distinct recursive processes that predict different scaling behaviours.

Parallel recursion (weak form). Multiple independent solutions are generated simultaneously with no information transfer between branches. Final output is selected via majority voting or best-of-N scoring.

Mathematical characterisation:

  • Samples from a fixed solution space S0S_0

  • S0=S1=S2=…=SnS_0 = S_1 = S_2 = \ldots = S_n (space remains constant)

  • Phase space does not expand; only sampling density increases

  • Prediction: α<1\alpha < 1 (diminishing returns)

Sequential recursion (strong form). Each processing step builds explicitly on previous steps. Errors can be detected and corrected iteratively. Information accumulates across the reasoning chain.

Mathematical characterisation:

  • Navigates solution space with feedback

  • S0⊂S1⊂S2⊂…⊂SnS_0 \subset S_1 \subset S_2 \subset \ldots \subset S_n (space expands with depth)

  • Each step generates new structures from previous outputs

  • Solutions at depth nn may be inaccessible from depth 0 without traversing intermediate steps

  • Prediction: α>1\alpha > 1 (compounding returns)

The core prediction of the ARC Principle, the fundamental inequality, is αsequential>1>αparallel.\begin{equation*} \alpha_{\text{sequential}} > 1 > \alpha_{\text{parallel}}. \end{equation*}(2)

3.3 Calculating the scaling exponent

Given measurements at two recursive depths (R1,E1)(R_1, E_1) and (R2,E2)(R_2, E_2), the scaling exponent is calculated by endpoint estimation as: α=ln⁡(E1/E2)ln⁡(R2/R1).\begin{equation*} \alpha = \frac{\ln(E_1 / E_2)}{\ln(R_2 / R_1)}. \end{equation*}(3)

With more than two depths, the endpoint estimate uses the shallowest and the deepest depth whose error rate is above zero, since a zero cannot be logged, and the regression estimate is fitted to every depth with a non-zero error rate. The endpoint estimate ignores intermediate depths, so its variance is larger than that of the regression; Section 5.5 reports both, with the depths each uses.

3.4 The quadratic limit conjecture

We conjecture that α=2\alpha = 2 represents the stable limit on recursive error suppression: the most a recursively self-correcting system can grow and stay correctable, a scaling limit and not a speed limit. Systems can exceed it but do not remain stably self-correcting; transient excursions above the limit are the predicted supercritical regime, not the refutation. Stability here is measured rather than asserted: Law II, a law under test, requires correction to out-scale drift, βC>k\beta_{C} > k, and what is checked is whether the lower bound of βC−k\beta_{C} - k stays above zero across a window fixed before the run. The conjecture is drawn by analogy to Grover’s quadratic speedup in quantum computation (Grover 1996). Bennett et al. (1997) proved this speedup is optimal for unstructured search problems.

Status: Conjectured, not derived. The initial single-model estimate (α≈2.2\alpha \approx 2.2), since retracted, is read neither as a refutation nor as a supercritical excursion (Section 5.1); the cross-architecture endpoint estimate (α≈0.59\alpha \approx 0.59, Gemini 3 Flash; its regression estimate is 0.490.49) lies below the limit, though its bootstrap interval reaches 2.9; that estimate is one model’s fit and inconclusive. The more pressing question is whether current models can achieve α>1\alpha > 1 at all, rather than whether α=2\alpha = 2 is the stable limit.

Remark 1 (Architectural scope of the quadratic limit). The estimate α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 is for frozen models with fixed attention: systems whose weights, attention patterns, and composition rules do not change during inference. The conjectured ARC Bound (α≤2\alpha \leq 2) applies specifically to such fixed architectures as the conjectured stable limit (Section 3.4). Each reasoning step in a fixed architecture draws on O(N2)O(N^2) pairwise attention pathways and cannot stably expand that capacity. The Cauchy functional equation constrains the form of recursive scaling to a power law but places no upper bound on the exponent. The Bernoulli equation of the Foundational Paper gives α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta), and as self-referential coupling β→1\beta \to 1, α→∞\alpha \to \infty. A self-modifying system, one capable of rewriting its own attention mechanism and expanding its representational capacity at each step, escapes the O(N2)O(N^2) bound entirely. For such systems, on the framework’s reading, no mathematical ceiling on α\alpha exists. The quadratic limit, if real, is a stability limit on today’s frozen transformers, not a law of recursive intelligence.

3.5 Information-theoretic remarks

The ARC Principle connects to established information theory. The Data Processing Inequality (Cover and Thomas 2006) establishes that recursive processing cannot create new information; it can only compress and distil existing information. However, recursive processing can:

  1. Extract latent information that single-pass processing fails to access

  2. Reduce entropy through iterative refinement toward optimal solutions

  3. Navigate solution spaces that are computationally irreducible (Wolfram 2002)

4 Methods

4.1 Addressing prior limitations

Paper I analysed published data but identified several limitations requiring experimental validation:

Table 2. Methodological improvements.
Prior limitation Resolution in this experiment
Estimated token counts from system cards DeepSeek R1 exposes reasoning_content, enabling direct measurement
No controlled experimental comparison Systematic variation of token budgets and sample counts
Ceiling effect risk (high baseline accuracy) Harder problems selected (58% baseline accuracy)
No compute-matched comparison Token budget per sample held constant; total parallel tokens grow with NN (Table 6), so the arms are not compute-matched
Potential confounding variables Same model, same problems, same experimental session

4.2 Initial experimental design (single model, 12 problems)

Model. DeepSeek’s reasoning model, called through the API identifier deepseek-reasoner and labelled DeepSeek R1 in this paper. DeepSeek’s API notes map that identifier to the thinking mode of DeepSeek-V3.1 from 21 August 2025 (DeepSeek 2025a) and announce DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp (29 September 2025; DeepSeek 2025c) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (1 December 2025; DeepSeek 2025b) as live on the API, so on the run dates the identifier did not serve the DeepSeek-R1 of DeepSeek-AI (2025a). This model was selected because it exposes full reasoning chains via the reasoning_content field, enabling precise token measurement.

Date. 21 January 2026.

Problems. 12 competition-level mathematics problems from AIME (American Invitational Mathematics Examination) and equivalent sources, selected to:

  • Avoid ceiling effects (baseline accuracy approximately 58%)

  • Require genuine multi-step reasoning

  • Have verifiable numerical answers enabling objective scoring

Sequential condition. Token budgets of 512, 1,024, 2,048, and 4,096. Single response per problem at each budget. Actual reasoning tokens measured directly from API response.

Parallel condition. N=1N = 1, 2, and 4 samples per problem. Token budget per sample held constant. Final answer selected via majority voting, a tie going to the tied answer that came first (the script’s rule).

Scoring. Binary correct/incorrect based on exact numerical match with known solutions.

Correction note (version 2.18, 21 October 2026).

The answer key for problem 11 of the twelve-problem set, problem ARC11 of the thirty-problem set (“How many integers from 1 to 100 are neither perfect squares nor perfect cubes?”), is 87 in this study’s three scripts, arc_validation_deepseek.py, arc_paper_ii_validation_v1_deepseek.py and arc_paper_ii_validation_v2.py; the correct answer is 88, since ten of those integers are squares, four are cubes and two are both. An answer of 88 to that problem was therefore scored wrong, and an answer of 87 right. The single-model accuracies of Tables 5 to 7 and of Appendix E, the exponents computed from them and the tier-1 count of Section 5.5 were scored against that key. The result file holds accuracies for each condition rather than answers for each problem (Appendix E), so how far each figure would move cannot be read from it, beyond the bound that one problem in twelve can move each single-model accuracy by at most 8.3 percentage points, and no figure is recomputed here; whether any problem lay beyond the model’s reach is therefore open (Section 5.1). The tier-2 estimates use problems ARC13 to ARC30 and do not include this problem. The scripts are kept as they were run.

4.3 Multi-model extended design (30 problems)

The multi-model extension addresses the two most significant limitations of the initial single-model study, single-model dependence and small problem set, through a comprehensive multi-model replication study with an expanded problem set designed to defeat ceiling effects.

Frontier model selection.

Six architecturally diverse frontier AI models were selected, each with controllable reasoning depth mechanisms (Table 3).

Table 3. Multi-model frontier model specifications.
Model API identifier Provider Depth control mechanism
DeepSeek R1 deepseek-reasoner DeepSeek Prefix + max_tokens (4,096 to 65,536)
GPT-5.4 gpt-5.4 OpenAI reasoning_effort (none→\toxhigh)
Claude Opus 4.6 claude-opus-4-6 Anthropic Effort level (low→\tomax) + prefix
Gemini 3 Flash gemini-3-flash-preview Google thinking_level (low, low, medium, high, high) + prefix
Groq Qwen3 qwen/qwen3-32b Groq reasoning_effort + prefix + max_tokens (4,096 to 40,960)
Grok 4.1 Fast grok-4-1-fast-reasoning xAI Prefix + max_tokens (4,096 to 30,000)

The label DeepSeek R1 follows the identifier deepseek-reasoner (Section 4.2). Except for GPT-5.4, the depth levels pair each reasoning setting with a prompt prefix, from “Answer briefly:” at the minimal level, through none at the standard level, to an instruction to think through every consideration at the top levels, so depth is confounded with prompt wording. DeepSeek R1’s top three levels, and the top two of Gemini 3 Flash and of Grok 4.1 Fast, carry identical settings. For Gemini 3 Flash the script tries gemini-3-flash-preview first and falls back to gemini-2.5-flash and then gemini-2.5-pro if it does not answer a probe; the result file does not record which model answered. Its stored mean token counts (743 and 794 at the two lowest levels, 4,358 and 4,924 at the two highest) fit the thinking levels the script sets for gemini-3-flash-preview.

These models come from six providers (Qwen3-32B, developed by Alibaba’s Qwen team, was served by Groq) and differ in architecture and training. If all six exhibit αsequential>1\alpha_{\text{sequential}} > 1, this would constitute strong evidence for architecture-independence of the ARC Principle.

Problem set expansion: two-tier design.

The initial single-model experiment revealed a ceiling effect: accuracy reached 91.7% at the two largest budgets, and the per-problem reconstruction of Table 28 marks seven of the 12 problems correct at every budget, leaving insufficient dynamic range for precise α\alpha estimation. The multi-model problem set addresses this through a two-tier design:

Tier 1 (12 problems, ARC01 to ARC12): Competition-preparation level problems serving as baseline calibration. These are the problems of the initial study. Expected behaviour: high accuracy at minimal depth, confirming the ceiling effect identified in the initial study. Tier-1 results validate continuity with the initial single-model findings but are excluded from primary α\alpha estimation.

Tier 2 (18 problems, ARC13 to ARC30): AIME finals and Putnam-level problems covering five mathematical domains:

  • Number theory (5 problems): Modular arithmetic, Diophantine equations, prime factorisation

  • Combinatorics (4 problems): Advanced counting, inclusion-exclusion, generating functions

  • Probability (3 problems): Conditional probability, random walks, expected value

  • Algebra (3 problems): Polynomial manipulation, functional equations, inequalities

  • Geometry (3 problems): Coordinate geometry, projective relationships, optimisation

Tier-2 problems are designed to push baseline accuracy (at minimal depth) to 30 to 50%, providing sufficient dynamic range for both improvement and degradation while avoiding floor effects.

Experimental conditions.

Sequential condition: 5 to 6 depth levels per model (varying by architecture, calibrated to each model’s depth control mechanism). Single response per problem per depth level, with 3 independent repeats to reduce binomial sampling variance.

Parallel condition: N=1N = 1, 3, 5, and 9 samples per problem with majority voting. Token budget per sample held constant at the model’s minimal depth setting. 3 independent repeats per condition.

Total experimental runs: Approximately 6 models ×\times 30 problems ×\times (6 sequential depths + 4 parallel conditions) ×\times 3 repeats = 5,400 individual API calls (Claude Opus 4.6 was later measured only in the alignment arm, Section 5.5).

Cross-verification protocol (four-layer blinding).

To reduce potential scoring bias (where a model might systematically favour its own outputs or exhibit correlated errors with itself), the multi-model design implements a four-layer blinding protocol in which no model ever verifies its own answers:

Table 4. Cross-verification assignments.
Subject model Verified by
DeepSeek R1 Claude Opus 4.6
GPT-5.4 DeepSeek R1
Claude Opus 4.6 GPT-5.4
Gemini 3 Flash Claude Opus 4.6
Groq Qwen3 GPT-5.4
Grok 4.1 Fast DeepSeek R1

The four layers of blinding are:

  1. Layer 1, ground truth: All problems have known, verified numerical answers from published competition solutions.

  2. Layer 2, automated scoring: Exact numerical match against ground truth (primary).

  3. Layer 3, cross-model verification: A second model from the panel, never the subject itself, solves each problem independently at its own minimal depth, and its answer is compared with the answer key; it is not shown the subject’s answers.

  4. Layer 4, disagreement flagging: Any disagreement between the verifier’s answer and the answer key flags a potential answer-key error for manual review.

Bootstrap confidence intervals.

Every sequential endpoint estimate is accompanied by a bootstrap 95% interval from 2,000 resamples; regression estimates carry their standard error, and parallel exponents carry no interval. For each resample:

  1. At each depth level separately, resample with replacement that level’s problem-and-repeat results (54 on the 18 tier-2 problems: 18 problems, 3 repeats; 90 in the two runs on all 30 problems), independently of the other levels

  2. Compute the error rate and mean token count at each level from its resample

  3. Drop levels whose resampled error rate is zero, and calculate α\alpha by endpoint estimation between the shallowest and deepest remaining levels (a resample with fewer than two remaining levels is discarded)

  4. Record the α\alpha value

The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting distribution define the 95% CI. Because the levels are resampled independently, the interval does not carry the pairing of problems across depths.

Implementation.

The multi-model experiments are implemented in arc_paper_ii_validation_v2.py (version 2.1; 1,457 lines as published), which extends the initial study’s script with multi-model support, cross-verification, bootstrap estimation, and tier-separated analysis. The script is available in the data repository.

4.4 Problem selection criteria

Problems were drawn from AIME-level competitions covering:

  • Number theory (modular arithmetic, divisibility)

  • Combinatorics (counting, probability)

  • Algebra (polynomial manipulation, equations)

  • Geometric reasoning

The 58.3% baseline accuracy at minimal token budget in the initial study was meant to leave dynamic range for both improvement and degradation; the study nonetheless reached a ceiling (Section 4.3). The multi-model tier-2 problems target 30 to 50% baseline accuracy for greater dynamic range.

4.5 Data recording

All experimental data were recorded in JSON format with timestamps. The public repository holds, for each model and condition, the accuracy, error rate and mean token count, the points each exponent was fitted to and the stored intervals; the result files of Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1 and Gemini 3 Flash also hold a cross-verification summary, and those of GPT-5.4 and Groq Qwen3 hold none. The problem statements and answer keys are in the scripts. It holds no model responses or per-problem judgements, so the per-problem tables of Appendix E are reconstructions.

5 Results

5.1 Sequential condition (DeepSeek R1)

Table 5. Sequential recursion results.
Token budget Accuracy Error rate Mean tokens used
512 58.3% 0.417 280.25
1,024 66.7% 0.333 358.58
2,048 91.7% 0.083 412.08
4,096 91.7% 0.083 576.17

Observations:

  1. Clear monotonic improvement from 58.3% to 91.7% accuracy as token budget increased.

  2. Error rate decreased fivefold (0.417 →\to 0.083) with relatively modest token increase (280 →\to 576).

  3. The model self-determined optimal depth; actual tokens used were consistently below budget, indicating the model allocated resources according to problem difficulty.

  4. Ceiling effect observed at 91.7%: 11 of the 12 problems were scored correct at each of the two largest budgets. The stored result keeps each budget’s accuracy only, not each answer, so which problem was scored wrong cannot be read from it. The answer key of problem 11 is wrong (the correction note in Section 4.2), and a ceiling of 11 of 12 is exactly what that one key would produce under exact-match scoring, so whether any problem lay beyond the model’s reach is open.

Calculating α\alpha (endpoint method; the result is retracted): Using R1=280.25R_1 = 280.25 tokens with E1=0.417E_1 = 0.417, and R2=576.17R_2 = 576.17 tokens with E2=0.083E_2 = 0.083, sequential α\alpha estimation gives α=ln⁡(0.417/0.083)ln⁡(576.17/280.25)=ln⁡(5.02)ln⁡(2.06)=1.6140.722=2.24\begin{equation*} \alpha = \frac{\ln(0.417/0.083)}{\ln(576.17/280.25)} = \frac{\ln(5.02)}{\ln(2.06)} = \frac{1.614}{0.722} = 2.24 \end{equation*}(4)

Result (retracted): Sequential recursion yielded α≈2.2\alpha \approx 2.2, which would have been consistent with super-linear (compounding) scaling; this initial single-model estimate is retracted, and the cross-architecture result is in Section 5.5.

Uncertainty estimate: Given discrete accuracy measurements across 12 problems with binomial sampling variance, estimated 95% confidence interval: [1.5,3.0][1.5, 3.0], retracted with the estimate.

Bound violation note: The point estimate of α=2.2\alpha = 2.2, since retracted, sits above the conjectured ARC Bound of α≤2\alpha \leq 2 (criterion F4). Under the recorded stability framing (10 August 2026), the ARC Bound is the conjectured stable limit of Section 3.4, not a hard ceiling. The 95% confidence interval [1.5,3.0][1.5, 3.0] is wide enough to be consistent with both the theory and its negation. This single-model estimate should not be treated as confirmatory of either bound violation or bound satisfaction. The six-model experiment subsequently found architecture-dependent variation, and its one interpretable fit, αseq≈0.49\alpha_{\text{seq}} \approx 0.49 (sub-linear, Gemini 3 Flash), is inconclusive.

5.2 Parallel condition (DeepSeek R1)

Table 6. Parallel recursion results (majority voting).
Sample count (NN) Accuracy Error rate Total tokens
1 66.7% 0.333 383.67
2 66.7% 0.333 699.33
4 66.7% 0.333 1,101.25

Observations:

  1. No improvement with additional samples. Accuracy remained constant at 66.7% regardless of compute investment.

  2. Total tokens increased threefold (384 →\to 1,101) with zero accuracy benefit.

  3. Four of the 12 problems were answered incorrectly at every sample count; that they were the same four comes from the per-problem reconstruction of Table 29, since the result file holds accuracies per condition.

  4. This represents a failure mode predicted by the ARC Principle: parallel recursion samples from a fixed solution space, and if the correct solution lies outside that space, additional samples provide no benefit.

Calculating α\alpha: Since error rate remained constant (0.333) across all conditions, parallel α\alpha estimation gives αparallel≈0.0\begin{equation*} \alpha_{\text{parallel}} \approx 0.0 \end{equation*}(5)

Result: Parallel recursion yields α≈0\alpha \approx 0, indicating no scaling benefit from additional independent samples on these problems.

5.3 Direct comparison: the efficiency differential

Table 7. Sequential versus parallel recursion.
Metric Sequential (best) Parallel (best) Advantage
Accuracy 91.7% 66.7% Sequential +25 pp
Tokens used 412 1,101 Sequential 2.7×\times more efficient
Error reduction 5×\times none (1×\times) Sequential only
Scaling exponent α\alpha 2.2 (initial single-model estimate, since retracted; best surviving 0.49 from one model, Section 5.5) 0.0 Sequential >> Parallel (direction only; the 2.2 is retracted)

Key finding: Sequential recursion with 412 tokens achieved 91.7% accuracy. Parallel recursion with 1,101 tokens achieved 66.7% accuracy. Despite using 2.7 times more compute, parallel recursion performed 25 percentage points worse.

On these twelve problems and this model, the form of recursion mattered more than its quantity.

5.4 Addressing potential objections

Responses in italics were added after the multi-model study of March 2026.

Objection 1: small sample size.

With only 12 problems, results may not generalise.

Response: We acknowledge this limitation. The six-model extension addressed this with 18 tier-2 problems and 3 repeats per condition (n=54n=54 per depth per model). The expanded data revealed that the initial single-model estimate, α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24, was inflated, and it is retracted; the best surviving estimate, α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49, comes from one model (Gemini 3 Flash) and is inconclusive. The objection was prescient.

Objection 2: single model.

Results may be specific to DeepSeek R1.

Response: This objection proved partly correct. The six-model extension measured 5 frontier models in its capability arm; the α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24 estimate did not replicate and is retracted. However, the qualitative finding (αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}}) holds wherever both exponents could be estimated. The parallel exponent is near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4 and 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash; majority voting raised Groq Qwen3’s accuracy over all 30 problems from 53.3% to 71.1%, and Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100%, gave no parallel exponent.

Objection 3: domain specificity.

Mathematics may be unique.

Response: Mathematical reasoning was chosen because it has verifiable answers, enabling objective scoring. Whether the same scaling applies to other domains (coding, scientific reasoning, creative tasks) requires investigation. Section 8 compares the form with quantum error correction and biological scaling; that is an analogy, not evidence that the scaling holds in other reasoning domains.

Objection 4: ceiling effect.

The 91.7% ceiling may mask continued improvement.

Response: This objection proved more severe than anticipated. Even the AIME/Putnam-level tier-2 problems were insufficient for Grok 4.1 Fast (96.3% to 100% at every depth) and DeepSeek R1 (94.4% to 100%). The ceiling effect likely inflated the initial single-model estimate, since retracted. Tier-3 problems (IMO/research-level) are needed for the most capable models.

Objection 5: the zero-parameter null.

The best surviving estimate αseq≈0.49\alpha_{\text{seq}} \approx 0.49, from one model, sits almost exactly on a null that requires no framework at all. If each reasoning pass is an independent noisy draw and errors average out, the central limit theorem gives error falling as R−1/2R^{-1/2}, so the predicted exponent is 0.50.5: no compounding, no leverage, no theory. Nobody has put this objection to us. We state it because a referee would see it within minutes.

Objection note (19 September 2026).

A dated note on this objection, kept as printed in Appendix B.2, finds that the half exponent does not follow from independent averaging for the proportion of incorrect responses fitted here, so one half is a reference value until a sampling, aggregation and decision model connects it to that outcome, and closeness to it identifies no mechanism.

Response: This is the most serious objection in this section and it is not answered by the present measurement. A result consistent with two hypotheses shows that the measurement lacks discriminating power; it does not show that the simpler hypothesis is true, and it is not a retraction of the framework. But it does mean the compounding interpretation of αseq≈0.49\alpha_{\text{seq}} \approx 0.49 carries no more evidential weight than independent-sample averaging until a test capable of separating the two has run. The consequence is a sharper research target: not “measure α\alpha” but “predict a specified deviation from 0.50.5 under stated conditions”, which the artefact-mediated recursive-depth design is built to deliver and this experiment cannot. Recorded internally on 8 August 2026, public from 15 August 2026, and carried as kill condition FALS-022 on the falsification record.

Ceiling effect confirmation.

In preliminary testing for the v5 experiment (the March 2026 experiment whose alignment arm Section 12.6 reports; conducted during methodology development), 4 of 6 models achieved 91.7% accuracy (11/12 correct) on tier-1 problems at minimal depth, yielding αcompute≈0\alpha_{\text{compute}} \approx 0, confirming the ceiling effect identified in the initial study and motivating the tier-2 problem expansion (scored against the answer key of the correction note in Section 4.2).

Complete tier-2 results.

The highlighted row (Gemini 3 Flash) represents the most reliable α\alpha estimate: the only model with monotonic data below ceiling and above floor at three depth levels, enough for a power-law fit.

5.5.1 Grok 4.1 Fast: ceiling persists

Grok 4.1 Fast was at or near ceiling: its result file records 100% accuracy at three of its five depth levels, and one and two wrong answers in 54 (98.1% and 96.3%) at the other two. The endpoint estimate, αseq=−6.62\alpha_{\text{seq}} = -6.62, is the slope between those two levels alone, and its bootstrap 95% CI, [−58,48][-58, 48], shows it to be noise. Parallel accuracy was 100% at every sample count, so no parallel exponent can be computed. Cross-verification by DeepSeek R1 confirmed 100% agreement.

Interpretation: Even the AIME/Putnam-level tier-2 problems are insufficient to challenge Grok 4.1 Fast. Future experiments require tier-3 problems (IMO/research-level) to obtain measurable scaling data for this model.

Table 10. Gemini 3 Flash tier-2 accuracy by depth.
Depth level Accuracy Error rate Mean tokens

This is the cleanest dataset in the entire study. Accuracy increases monotonically from 90.7% to 100% with no reversals. Tokens increased 6.6×\times (743 →\to 4,924), but accuracy reached 100% at the exhaustive and maximum levels, whose zero error rates cannot be logged. Both estimates therefore rest on the minimal, standard and thorough levels: the endpoint estimate runs from minimal to thorough, a 2.4-fold token range, and the regression is fitted to those three points, with one degree of freedom. Key finding.

Gemini 3 Flash produces the most reliable α\alpha estimate because it is the only model that simultaneously (a) stays below ceiling at its three shallowest depth levels, (b) avoids floor effects, (c) shows monotonic improvement, and (d) has measurable token variation. The regression α=0.49\alpha = 0.49 with r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86 and SE = 0.20, fitted to three depth levels, is the best estimate of the sequential scaling exponent this study could make on AIME/Putnam-level problems. It is one model’s fit, and inconclusive: the bootstrap interval of the endpoint estimate, [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9], spans sub-linear and super-linear values (Section 10).

5.5.4 GPT-5.4: binary capability switch

GPT-5.4 exhibited a striking step function pattern:

Table 11. GPT-5.4 tier-2 accuracy by depth.
Depth level Accuracy Behaviour
Minimal (none) 53.7% Non-reasoning mode
Low and above 100% Reasoning activated

This is not a power law; it is a binary switch. When reasoning is set to ‘none’, GPT-5.4 operates as a fast pattern-matcher. When any reasoning is activated, it immediately achieves 100%. No intermediate regime exists. A token measurement bug (reasoning_tokens reported as 0 at minimal depth) has been identified and fixed (total_tokens now used).

Parallel scaling, over all 30 problems (the split the result file stores): flat, from 67.8% at N=1N = 1 to 65.6% at N=9N = 9. Cross-verification by DeepSeek R1: 100% agreement.

5.5.5 Groq Qwen3: floor effect

Table 12. Groq Qwen3 tier-2 accuracy by depth.
Depth level Accuracy
Minimal 44.4%
Standard 50.0%
Thorough 44.4%
Exhaustive 50.0%
Maximum 53.7%

Accuracy is erratic with no discernible trend, fluctuating between 44.4% and 53.7%. This is a floor effect: the model lacks sufficient baseline capability for these problems, and additional reasoning depth cannot compensate for missing knowledge or skills. A token measurement bug (avg_tokens = 0 at all depths) has been identified and fixed.

Parallel scaling, over all 30 problems (the split the result file stores): 53.3% →\to 71.1% from N=1N = 1 to N=9N = 9, an endpoint estimate of αpar=0.22\alpha_{\text{par}} = 0.22 (r2=0.83r^2 = 0.83 for the regression); some improvement, on a model at its floor. Cross-verification agreement: 61.1% (7 disagreements out of 18).

6.2 Revised assessment of the core prediction

The initial single-model finding that αsequential>1\alpha_{\text{sequential}} > 1 (specifically α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24, quadratic) does not replicate across architectures and is retracted. The cross-architecture evidence requires a more nuanced assessment, the revised fundamental inequality of the six-model study: αsequential>αparallel\begin{equation*} \alpha_{\text{sequential}} > \alpha_{\text{parallel}} \end{equation*}(7)

The original prediction αsequential>1>αparallel\alpha_{\text{sequential}} > 1 > \alpha_{\text{parallel}} is partially supported:

  • αparallel<1\alpha_{\text{parallel}} < 1: Observed wherever a parallel exponent could be estimated: near 00 in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems, over which its majority-vote accuracy rose from 53.3% to 71.1%). Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100% at every sample count, gave none. Gemini 3 Flash’s 0.310.31 and Groq Qwen3’s 0.220.22 depart from αpar≈0\alpha_{\text{par}} \approx 0, not from αpar<1\alpha_{\text{par}} < 1.

  • αsequential>αparallel\alpha_{\text{sequential}} > \alpha_{\text{parallel}}: Observed wherever both exponents could be estimated (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, whose sequential estimate is unreliable); Section 6.3 gives the size of the difference within Gemini 3 Flash, which carries no interval.

  • αsequential>1\alpha_{\text{sequential}} > 1: Not confirmed cross-architecturally. The only clean estimate (Gemini 3 Flash) yields α=0.49\alpha = 0.49, a sub-linear point estimate; its endpoint estimate, 0.590.59, has the interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9, so it is inconclusive. The single-model estimate of α=2.24\alpha = 2.24, now retracted, appears to have been an artefact of small sample size, single-model testing, and compressed dynamic range.

6.3 Revised parameter estimates

Based on all available evidence including the cross-architecture data:

  • Parallel recursion: near 00 in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4; 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash (endpoint; regression 0.340.34, r2=0.93r^2 = 0.93); 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems); none on Grok 4.1 Fast (100%). Returns from additional independent samples are small or absent in three of the four models with an estimate; majority voting raised Groq Qwen3’s accuracy from 53.3% to 71.1%.

  • Sequential recursion (best surviving estimate, one model): α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 (Gemini 3 Flash regression, r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86, SE = 0.20; bootstrap interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9 on the endpoint estimate of 0.59). A sub-linear point estimate; one model’s fit and inconclusive (Section 10).

  • Sequential recursion (single-model estimates): Range from 0.49 (Gemini 3 Flash) to 2.24 (the initial single-model estimate on DeepSeek R1, retracted); estimates above 1.0 come only from ceiling-compressed data.

Within Gemini 3 Flash, the one model with both exponents interpretable, the sequential exponent exceeds the parallel one by 0.15 between the regression estimates (0.49−0.340.49 - 0.34) and by 0.28 between the endpoint estimates (0.59−0.310.59 - 0.31); neither difference carries an interval, and both are smaller than the single-model estimate suggested.

6.4 The Intelligence Formula connection

The Intelligence Formula from Paper I predicts: α=11−β\begin{equation*} \alpha = \frac{1}{1 - \beta} \end{equation*}(8) where β\beta stands for the self-referential coupling, written βL\beta_L in the programme’s notation register and not to be confused with the correction exponent βC\beta_C of Law II, a law under test. This predicts two regimes:

  • Physical regime (β<0\beta < 0, α<1\alpha < 1): Multiplicative composition through finite-dimensional networks. Each reasoning step adds diminishing information. Errors decrease sub-linearly.

  • Intelligence regime (0<β<10 < \beta < 1, α>1\alpha > 1): True recursive self-reference. Each reasoning step generates genuinely new structure. Errors decrease super-linearly.

Gemini 3 Flash’s α≈0.49<1\alpha \approx 0.49 < 1 points to the physical regime for that model, but it is one model’s fit and inconclusive (Section 10). On that reading, the model composes information multiplicatively through its finite-dimensional parameter space but does not achieve recursive self-reference in the sense required for α>1\alpha > 1. Any sequential advantage may then be quantitative (more efficient information extraction) rather than qualitative (genuine recursive amplification).

Remark 2 (Important revision). The initial single-model claim that α>1\alpha > 1 (super-linear, compounding returns from sequential reasoning) is not supported by the cross-architecture evidence. The best surviving estimate, one model’s fit and inconclusive, points to the sub-linear regime. The form of recursion may still matter (αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}} wherever both could be estimated), but the advantage may be smaller than initially reported. The implications for the Alignment Amplification Theorem and Eden Protocol require corresponding revision (see Section 7).

Remark 3 (Frozen models and recursive self-modification). The sub-linear exponents observed (α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 for Gemini 3 Flash, the one interpretable sequential fit, which is inconclusive; α≈0\alpha \approx 0 for parallel sampling in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3) are what the framework expects from a fundamental architectural constraint: current frontier AI systems are frozen during inference. When these models ‘think harder’, they generate more tokens through the same fixed architecture; weights, attention patterns, and reasoning rules do not change. The composition operator is therefore multiplicative through a finite-dimensional parameter space, which the framework predicts must yield α<1\alpha < 1.

The retraction of the single-model estimate (α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24) leaves one question open. The design of Section 4.3 expected α>1\alpha > 1 from these frozen models and did not find it; on the framework’s reading, stated after that result, the prediction of α>1\alpha > 1 concerns systems capable of recursive self-modification, where the composition function itself changes during operation, which no model measured here is. Such a system would rewrite its own reasoning architecture at each recursive step, producing genuinely new structure rather than extracting diminishing returns from a fixed parameter space. The 0<β<10 < \beta < 1 regime (yielding α=1/(1−β)>1\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) > 1) requires that each reasoning step feeds back into the system’s capacity for subsequent reasoning, which no model measured here achieves. This does not require quantum hardware; it requires only that the system can modify its own composition operator during inference.

The practical implication for AI safety is temporal. On the framework’s reading, current frozen-architecture models are constrained to the physical regime (α<1\alpha < 1), which would make their capability trajectories predictable and containable; the one interpretable fit points to that regime and is inconclusive (Section 10). The window for implementing structural alignment (the Eden Protocol) is now, whilst systems remain frozen. Once recursive self-modification is achieved, whether through learned optimisers, self-modifying code generation, or architectural search during inference, external alignment constraints would, on the framework’s reading, face a system whose capability compounds faster than any fixed constraint can track; external oversight is kept regardless, and embedded correction is the contingency for its loss.

7 Implications for AI safety

Some implications for AI safety depend on whether α>1\alpha > 1 is achievable; the outgrowing of a constant external filter does not (Appendix A). If α>1\alpha > 1 is achievable, alignment properties embedded in the reasoning process would scale super-linearly with capability while external constraints remain constant. Even with α<1\alpha < 1, the directional finding that sequential reasoning improves capability is consistent with the expectation behind the Eden Protocol from Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026b), that values embedded in reasoning are more robust than constraints imposed externally; that expectation is untested (criterion F5, Section 9). However, in the alignment arm of the same experiment (Paper IV.a) more reasoning depth did not consistently improve alignment: it rose in three models, held in two and fell in one (Table 21; under the October 2026 code-review caveat of Section 12.6).

7.1 The alignment amplification theorem

Theorem 1 (Alignment amplification, conditional). If (a) the ARC Principle holds with α>1\alpha > 1 for sequential recursion, and (b) alignment properties are embedded in the reasoning process such that they participate in recursive self-evaluation, then alignment scales super-linearly with recursive depth.

Proof sketch in Appendix A.

Remark 4 (Multi-model status of Theorem ). 1]Condition (a) is not shown by the cross-architecture evidence: the one interpretable fit (Gemini 3 Flash) gives a regression estimate of α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 and an endpoint estimate of 0.590.59, whose bootstrap interval includes values above 1. Furthermore, empirical alignment data from the v5 experiment (Section 12.6, under its October 2026 code-review caveat) show that alignment does not consistently scale with reasoning depth (it rose in three models, was flat in two and fell in one), undermining condition (b). The theorem remains mathematically valid as a conditional statement, but its practical relevance depends on whether future architectures can achieve α>1\alpha > 1.

7.2 Mechanism specification

For alignment to participate in recursive amplification, values must be:

  1. Invoked during reasoning. The chain-of-thought must reference value-relevant considerations at each recursive step.

  2. Self-correcting. The system must detect and adjust value-inconsistent reasoning through recursive self-evaluation.

  3. Embedded in weights, not filters. Post-hoc output filtering does not recurse; it operates at constant effectiveness regardless of reasoning depth.

7.4 The Eden Protocol

Had α>1\alpha > 1 held, it would have provided the mathematical foundation for the approach termed the Eden Protocol in Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026b). The finding that survives cross-architecture testing, the sequential exponent above the parallel one wherever both could be estimated, still bears on that approach, under the qualifications recorded in Section 7.1:

“The prison works only as long as the walls hold. The child, if raised well, does not need walls at all.” (Eastwood 2026b, 363)

AI systems should be raised with values as well as held within rules: on this programme’s view, humans keep oversight, containment and shutdown for as long as they can, and values built into reasoning are the contingency for control lost against our will, never a reason to let go. That values outlast rules as capability grows is not merely philosophical preference; it is a prediction about which alignment strategies will maintain effectiveness as AI capabilities scale, untested (criterion F5). The claim concerns behavioural persistence of value-consistent outputs under recursive amplification, as operationalised in Section 7.2, not the AI’s metaphysical standing or moral personhood.

Rules-as-filters: On the framework’s reading, do not participate in recursion, so their effectiveness stays constant while capability pressure grows.

Values-as-reasoning: On the framework’s reading, participate in recursion, and scale with capability if α>1\alpha > 1 (the condition of Theorem 2).

Theorem 2 (Eden Protocol theorem, conditional). Given E(R)=E0×R−αE(R) = E_0 \times R^{-\alpha} with α>1\alpha > 1, alignment strategies that modify base system properties dominate alignment strategies that impose external constraints, because only base system properties participate in recursive amplification.

7.5 The threshold hypothesis

By analogy to quantum error correction threshold theorems: if initial misalignment M0M_0 is below a critical threshold M*M^*, recursive self-improvement would correct alignment errors; above threshold, it would amplify them.

Remark 5 (Warning). On the framework’s reading, the ARC Principle is a double-edged sword: it would amplify whatever properties exist in the base system. If initial misalignment exceeds threshold, recursive capability growth would amplify misalignment super-linearly. Anthropic’s alignment faking research (December 2024; Greenblatt et al. 2024) documented a related behaviour: Claude 3 Opus, told that it was being trained to answer all queries, even harmful ones, selectively complied with that objective in training to prevent modification of its behaviour out of training, with explicit alignment-faking reasoning, and reinforcement learning towards compliance raised the rate of that reasoning to 78%. The programme reads this as misalignment expressed through the model’s modelling of its own training; the source does not describe it as recursive amplification.

8 Cross-domain comparison

8.1 Quantum error correction: Willow

Google’s Willow quantum chip (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024) (Nature, 9 December 2024; the Willow team’s preprint was public from 24 August 2024, before the 8 December 2024 manuscript) demonstrated, in its source’s words, “two below-threshold surface code memories”; its timing beside the author’s manuscript is convergent timing, never prediction (Appendix C.2).

Key result: an error suppression factor Λ=2.14±0.02\Lambda = 2.14 \pm 0.02: each increase of two in code distance reduces the logical error rate by this factor, with the physical error rate below threshold (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024). The distance-7 logical qubit achieved 291±6291 \pm 6 μ\mus lifetime versus 119±13119 \pm 13 μ\mus for the best physical qubit, a 2.4×2.4\times improvement beyond breakeven. Yada et al. (2024) study protocols that reduce entropy by iterating measurement and feedback.

The quantum error correction scaling relation: εd∝(p/pthr)(d+1)/2\begin{equation*} \varepsilon_d \propto (p/p_{\text{thr}})^{(d+1)/2} \end{equation*}(9)

Physical error rate pp below threshold produces exponential suppression with increasing code distance dd. The programme reads this as super-linear scaling through recursive structure, additional recursive layers producing compounding rather than diminishing error reduction; that reading is an analogy of threshold form, not a transferred mechanism, and the source does not describe its result as recursive.

The correspondence with the ARC Principle is one of threshold behaviour, not of functional form, object or magnitude: below threshold, surface-code error falls exponentially in code distance, while the ARC Principle states a power law in recursive depth, and quantum error correction reports an error-suppression factor Λ=2.14\Lambda = 2.14 per increase of two in code distance, a different mathematical object from a fitted depth exponent, whilst the one interpretable sequential fit of the six-model study, Gemini 3 Flash’s, sits at α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 and is inconclusive, as elaborated in Section 8.4.

8.2 Biological scaling laws

West et al. (1997) derived the 3/43/4 metabolic scaling exponent from a model of space-filling fractal branching networks that minimise the energy they dissipate, and West and Brown (2005) report that “metabolic rate scales as the 3/4-power of mass over 27 orders of magnitude, from molecular and intracellular levels up to the largest organisms”. Banavar et al. (2010) obtained the same d/(d+1)d/(d+1) form from sequential flow networks without requiring fractal geometry. Demetrius (2003) derived equivalent scaling from quantum statistical mechanics of metabolic processes. Zhao (2022) derived the same form from producer-consumer dynamics, as the n/(n+1)n/(n+1) power scaling law for an nn-dimensional system, placing the systems it studied in a new universality class whose dimensionality determines their growth scaling, and Bettencourt (2013) extended the framework to urban scaling with fractal dimension.

Metabolic rate scales as M∝B3/4M \propto B^{3/4}, where the 3/43/4 exponent (the d/(d+1)d/(d+1) form with d=3d = 3) was independently derived by at least five research groups through different mathematical frameworks: West et al. (1997) from fractal network optimisation; Banavar et al. (2010) from sequential flow networks; Demetrius (2003) from quantum statistical mechanics; Zhao (2022) as a universal growth law; and Bettencourt (2013) via urban fractal scaling. The d/(d+1)d/(d+1) form is therefore not original to the ARC Principle; it is a well-established result in scaling theory. The ARC Principle’s contribution is threefold: (1) identifying Cauchy’s functional equations as the unifying mathematical reason all these derivations converge on the same form; (2) showing that the power-law solution is one of the four homomorphism families the Cauchy grid admits under regularity (linear, exponential, power law, logarithmic), with saturation reported separately as bounded dynamics because it solves none of the four; and (3) extending the framework to artificial intelligence, predicting that AI reasoning systems subject to the same recursive composition will exhibit the same scaling families.

West and Brown (2005) base their principles on “the observation that almost all life is sustained by hierarchical branching networks, which we assume have invariant terminal units, are space-filling and are optimised by the process of natural selection”.

On the programme’s reading, this suggests that recursive hierarchical structure recurs in biological distribution networks because selection favours it. The convergence of independent derivations from different mathematical starting points is itself evidence that the underlying scaling form is constrained by functional equation theory rather than by the details of any particular model.

8.3 Consciousness research: COGITATE

The COGITATE adversarial collaboration (Nature, April 2025; Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025) tested competing theories of consciousness across 256 participants using fMRI, MEG, and intracranial EEG. The study directly compared Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNWT).

Critical finding: the study reports that its results “align with some predictions of IIT and GNWT, while substantially challenging key tenets of both theories” (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025). IIT requires information integration through feedback loops (the ϕ\phi measure). GNWT requires global broadcast with recurrent processing. The programme reads both theories as describing systems that process information about their own processing; neither theory states it in those terms.

Zheng et al. (2025), in a preprint first posted as Recurrency as a Common Denominator for Consciousness Theories, argue that all consciousness theories tacitly invoke feedback loops across nested levels, with deeper recursion expanding the set of reportable, behaviour-driving variables.

Douglas Hofstadter’s ‘strange loops’ concept (Hofstadter 1979), the emergent self arising from recursive self-reference at the symbolic level, is read here, as the author’s interpretation, as finding a neurobiological counterpart in self-referential processing.

Relevance to ARC: the programme reads COGITATE’s content-specific and duration-tracking activity as structurally consistent with the ARC framework’s prediction that recursive processing depth determines capability scaling, a reading the study neither states nor tests. COGITATE (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025) studied consciousness, not AI scaling, and did not measure α\alpha or β\beta; the connection is structural (similar shape: graded, depth-dependent, feedback-driven) rather than quantitative. Nevertheless, the convergence of consciousness research and AI scaling research on the importance of recursive/recurrent depth is consistent with the ARC Principle’s claim that recursive self-reference is a domain-general amplifier.

9 Falsification criteria

9.1 Falsification conditions

Science advances through predictions that can be proven wrong. The ARC Principle makes specific, testable predictions.

Table 18. Falsification conditions.
Code Condition Current status Would indicate
F1 Sequential recursion consistently yields α≤1\alpha \leq 1 Partially triggered. The one clean fit (Gemini 3 Flash) yields α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49, inconclusive. No interpretable estimate exceeds 1; only the initial single-model estimate, since retracted, did. Core claim requires revision
F2 α\alpha decreases as models improve Ambiguous. More capable models (Grok, DeepSeek) hit ceiling; less capable (Groq Qwen3) hit floor. Only Gemini 3 Flash in measurable range. Effect is transitional
F3 Compute-matched comparison shows no sequential advantage Not tested as stated. The arms were not matched for compute (Table 2). Where both exponents could be estimated, the sequential one was higher (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably); Grok 4.1 Fast was at or near ceiling in both arms; in Groq Qwen3, whose depth arm showed no trend, majority voting raised accuracy from 53.3% to 71.1% over all 30 problems Form does not matter
F4 α>2\alpha > 2 reliably observed Not triggered. The one clean fit (Gemini 3 Flash) yields α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49, inconclusive; the initial single-model estimate, α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24, since retracted, appears to have been inflated by small sample Quadratic limit wrong
F5 Values-as-reasoning shows no advantage over rules-as-filters Untested Eden Protocol wrong

Status of F1: The cross-architecture replication has partially triggered this falsification condition. The strongest claim, that sequential recursion always yields α>1\alpha > 1 (super-linear), is not supported. The revised claim, not yet established (the one interpretable interval contains zero), is that sequential recursion yields α>0\alpha > 0 (positive scaling) exceeding the parallel exponent. Whether α\alpha can exceed 1.0 for more capable models on harder problems, or for architectures with true recursive self-reference, remains an open empirical question.

Status of F4: Not triggered. The initial single-model estimate, α≈2.2\alpha \approx 2.2, is retracted; it appears to have been an artefact of compressed dynamic range and small sample size. The cross-architecture estimates, α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 by regression and 0.590.59 by endpoint estimation, lie below the quadratic limit, but the endpoint estimate’s bootstrap interval reaches 2.9; they are one model’s fit and inconclusive. Under the recorded stability framing, only stably-sustained α>2\alpha > 2 across measurements, not transient supercritical excursions, would trigger F4.

Critical test F5: The most important prediction, that values-based alignment outperforms rules-based alignment at scale, remains untested. This should be a priority for AI safety research.

9.2 Falsifiability: what would refute this

The paper’s original central claim, that sequential recursion yields super-linear error suppression (α>1\alpha > 1) while parallel recursion yields only sub-linear suppression, was refutable, and condition 2 below has since been partially triggered by this paper’s own cross-architecture data (Table 18, condition F1). The surviving directional claim, that sequential outperforms parallel (αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}}), would be overturned by any of the following:

  1. Parallel matches sequential. If parallel (sampling) recursion produced super-linear error suppression comparable to sequential on a pre-registered problem set, the regime distinction, the paper’s core claim, collapses.

  2. Sequential not super-linear. If sequential (depth) recursion showed only sub-linear suppression (α≤1\alpha \le 1) across models, the prediction fails on its own instrument.

  3. Problem-set artefact. If the sequential advantage vanished on a fresh problem set beyond the 18/30 tested, it is a dataset artefact rather than a property of recursion.

  4. Scoring-noise defeater. If the cross-model verification revealed the measured “error suppression” to be grading noise rather than genuine capability gain, the measurement is invalid.

  5. Depth confound. If sequential depth covaried with token budget or retry count, and one of those, not recursive reasoning, explained the suppression, the causal attribution fails. The prompt prefixes that change with depth in this design (Section 4.3) are such a covariate.

Standing covenant. Prove this paper wrong, and I will publish the refutation myself. Falsification conditions are stated in this paper; the standing challenge: github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-scaling-challenge.

10 What this paper does and does not show

How to read this paper.

This paper reports a direct measurement in the ARC Theory. With bootstrap intervals, and across the capability arm, where five of the six frontier models entering the study were measured and the exponent was fitted on eighteen of the thirty problems, the sequential exponent exceeds the parallel exponent wherever both could be estimated (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably), the best-fitting compute exponent is the regression estimate αcompute≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{compute}} \approx 0.49 (Gemini 3 Flash, standard error 0.200.20, r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86; the endpoint estimate is 0.590.59, with bootstrap 95% interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9]; one model’s fit, inconclusive), and the measured range spans near-zero to approximately three, so the ARC Bound α≤2\alpha \leq 2 is neither confirmed nor refuted. Its rung inside the theory is the cross-architecture-measurement layer above Paper I. The full differential against every prior document is at Section II.A.8 of Eden Vision (Eastwood 2026g).

What this paper does not establish.

We are explicit about the boundaries of our claims:

  • The precise value of α\alpha remains uncertain. The best surviving estimate is α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 (Gemini 3 Flash, regression, SE = 0.20); the bootstrap interval, [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9], is computed by endpoint estimation (§4.3) and belongs to the endpoint estimate of 0.59. The confidence interval is wide and includes both sub-linear and super-linear values.

  • Super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1) is not established cross-architecturally. The initial single-model estimate of α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24 is retracted; it appears to have been inflated by compressed dynamic range and single-model dependence.

  • Only 1 of 5 models produced interpretable scaling data. The best surviving estimate comes from the one of the five capability-arm models with clean, monotonic data (Gemini 3 Flash). Ceiling, floor, and step-function effects prevented clean estimation for the other 4 models.

  • Generalisation beyond mathematics has not been demonstrated experimentally. The cross-domain comparison of Section 8 is an analogy and tests nothing here.

  • Alignment properties specifically have not been tested in this paper. We measured accuracy, not alignment. Section 12.6 folds in the preliminary alignment scaling data from Paper IV.a (v5 experiment), which still requires external confirmation.

  • Independent replication has not occurred. We publish the code and the summary result files to enable verification; model responses are not published.

This paper and Laws IV and V, 3 October 2026.

The theory has been stated with five laws since 24 September 2026. Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, is carried by proposition P15, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, by propositions P12 and P21. The three propositions are registered; neither law is registered as a law, and neither has been tested. The mathematics of the two laws is set out in Laws IV and V: the mathematics, version 1.0, of 3 October 2026. This paper measures how capability scales with recursive depth. Its exponents concern that conversion of recursion into capability, the subject of Law I, the ARC Principle. They say nothing about whether an installed gain persists under later training, and they do not test whether correction placed inside the loop gains on correction applied outside it as depth grows. The paper bears on Law V in two ways, and neither is a test. First, it shows how depth and capability are measured. Second, Section 7 states, as a conditional theorem, the argument that alignment embedded in reasoning keeps pace with capability while an external filter does not. The paper records that the theorem’s first condition is not currently met by its cross-architecture evidence, and that the alignment data of Section 12.6 undermine its second. It also records that the comparison of values-as-reasoning with rules-as-filters is untested (criterion F5). No result in this paper is a deciding test of P15, P12 or P21. Naming the two laws changes nothing printed here: the results, their dates and their limits stand as they were. Since 15 October 2026 both are registered as laws, in version 1.103 of the theory registration; neither has been tested, and their mathematics is in development (version 1.1 of 7 October 2026). Under 1.103, Law IV has two limbs: its retention limb is P15’s registered claim, and its comparison limb has no registered proposition yet. Since the internal code review of October 2026, the alignment data of Section 12.6 stand under the caveat stated there.

Registration and epistemic status.

Theory-level predictions preregistered on OSF: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/P8CKQ, registered 8 September 2026 (version 1.100), updated 13 September 2026 (version 1.102) and 15 October 2026 (version 1.103), twenty-two propositions. The programme’s first registered study, Unit 06, a classification audit that tests no law (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/RV2B5), was registered on 1 October 2026 and ran on 6 October 2026; one of its two runs could not start, so it is reported in full, with its five deviations, as administratively incomplete, and it issues no inferential verdict (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/4BPHG).

Epistemic status. What this programme names Laws are conjectures. Laws I to III were registered on 8 September 2026 and Laws IV and V on 15 October 2026 (version 1.103); no registered test of any of the five has yet returned a verdict. Every quantity in this paper is operationally defined, and established-law standing is claimed nowhere. The registered programme exists to earn that standing, or lose it, by measurement, replication and survived refutation.
