Depth confounded with prompt wording High Every model except GPT-5.4 received a prompt prefix that changes with the depth level; no condition separates the prefix from the reasoning setting (Section 4.3).
Answer key of problem ARC11 set at 87 in the scripts, where the answer is 88 Low for the tier-2 estimates; affects the single-model figures and the tier-1 count Disclosed in Section 4.2; no figure recomputed, scripts kept as run

11.2 Two unchecked assumptions about the arms

The headline contrast in this paper is between a sequential arm and a parallel arm, and the result is reported as though those two words name what a reader takes them to name. They name it only under conditions of which this paper reports no check, and the conditions are not decorative: if either fails, the measured difference is a difference between labels rather than between mechanisms.

Three properties are usually collapsed into the word sequential, and only the third can produce an exponent. Order is an index, and parallel sampling has one too, since any set of independent samples can be numbered. Conditioning is each step seeing the previous step’s output. Retention is each step keeping something from the previous step that makes the next one better. A chain that conditions without retaining re-derives its position at every step and arrives where it started, which is parallel sampling performed in series: it looks like depth on a timeline and behaves like breadth in the result. And retention alone is still not enough. A chain can carry a state that is genuinely load-bearing and entirely static, in which case severing it removes the advantage while the advantage does not grow with depth, and the curve is a level shift followed by a flat line rather than a power law. What a scaling exponent stands on is accumulation, which is retention whose contribution grows with depth.

The parallel arm carries the mirror assumption. For a breadth measurement to be a breadth measurement, no output may be conditioned on any other at the moment it is generated. Aggregation after generation is permitted, including best-of-n selection, the standard breadth method; what is not permitted is a pipeline in which one sample sees another before it is produced. A breadth arm that conditions at generation time is not breadth at all, so an exponent measured on it is not a breadth exponent, whichever way it points. The programme’s theory registration now makes the condition a validity requirement: the study that will decide the depth and breadth comparison must demonstrate it on the pipeline it registers, and without that demonstration a result in which breadth compounds as depth does is recorded as not evaluable rather than as a refutation.

This paper reports no check of either condition, so its contrast is reported as provisional on both. What would settle the first is an ablation rather than an argument: sever what one step passes to the next, show the advantage goes with it, and run that severance at two depths, because a constant removed advantage is retention without accumulation. The programme’s theory registration requires the study that will decide the depth and breadth comparison to show, by inspecting its pipeline before any outcome is read, that what each step produces reaches the step after it; the severance is run at two depths fixed in advance and reported beside the result as evidence about mechanism, never as a gate in front of it. For the programme’s own measurement the direction is reported and the mechanism is not established.

12 Discussion

12.1 Why sequential recursion might scale differently from parallel sampling

The mathematical explanation centres on solution space geometry, the fixed and expanding solution spaces of Section 3.2.

Parallel recursion (fixed space). Each independent sample draws from the same solution space S0S_0. Additional samples increase sampling density but cannot access solutions outside S0S_0. If the correct solution is not in S0S_0, no amount of parallel sampling will find it.

Sequential recursion (expanding space). Each recursive step generates new structures from previous outputs. Solutions at step nn may be computationally irreducible, inaccessible from step 0 without traversing intermediate steps. The solution space expands with recursive depth.

This geometric difference is the mechanism by which sequential recursion could produce compounding returns (α>1\alpha > 1) while parallel recursion produces diminishing or zero returns. On the problems measured here the one interpretable sequential estimate was sub-linear and inconclusive (Section 12.5), so the mechanism’s super-linear form remains unconfirmed.

12.2 The DeepSeek ‘aha moment’ phenomenon

An intermediate version of DeepSeek-R1-Zero exhibits a documented phenomenon in which it rethinks its approach mid-solution (DeepSeek-AI 2025a, Table 3):

“Wait, wait. Wait. That’s an aha moment I can flag here.”

The source describes the model learning to “allocate more thinking time to a problem by reevaluating its initial approach”; the programme reads this as solution space expansion. The model generates an initial solution path, recognises inadequacy through recursive self-evaluation, and accesses a new solution space previously inaccessible from the initial framing.

Critically, in DeepSeek-R1-Zero this behaviour emerged through pure reinforcement learning without supervised fine-tuning; the model learned to allocate more thinking time. This suggests recursive self-improvement may be an attractor state for sufficiently capable learning systems.

12.3 Relationship to theoretical frameworks

The ARC Principle connects to established theoretical frameworks:

Friston’s Free Energy Principle. Friston (2010) casts brain function as the minimisation of free energy; the programme reads that as recursive prediction-error minimisation. The ARC Principle may be a computational instantiation: recursion is the mechanism through which systems minimise free energy by iteratively refining their world models.

Hofstadter’s Strange Loops. The emergent ‘I’ arising from self-referential recursive processing at the symbolic level (Hofstadter 1979). The ARC Principle formalises the scaling properties of such loops, predicting that deeper self-reference produces greater coherence.

Wolfram’s Computational Irreducibility. Certain computational processes cannot be predicted without running them step by step (Wolfram 2002). Sequential recursion may be the computational architecture that navigates irreducible solution spaces.

12.4 Relationship to Infinite Architects

This experimental work bears on the theoretical framework developed in Infinite Architects: Intelligence, Recursion, and the Creation of Everything (Eastwood 2026b):

  • ‘The Architecture of Mind’ articulated the core principle that recursive self-reference amplifies intelligence.

  • ‘The HRIH’ (the Hyperspace Recursive Intelligence Hypothesis) argued that consciousness emerges from recursive self-modelling, a claim structurally consistent with (though not directly tested by) the COGITATE findings (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025).

  • ‘The Eden Protocol’ argued for values-based over rules-based AI alignment. Section 7.1 states the Alignment Amplification Theorem as a conditional: if the ARC Principle holds with α>1\alpha > 1 for sequential recursion and alignment is embedded in the reasoning process, alignment scales super-linearly with recursive depth. This paper does not find condition (a) in the cross-architecture evidence, and the alignment data of Section 12.6, which stand under the October 2026 code-review caveat stated there, undermine condition (b).

  • ‘The Chokepoint’ analysed hardware governance through semiconductor manufacturing concentration, relevant to implementing the Eden Protocol at scale.

  • Embedded correction: the book sets out hardware-level safety mechanisms, relevant to preventing recursive amplification of misalignment.

The book provides broader philosophical context and practical implications; this paper provides mathematical formalisation and experimental tests.

12.5 Cross-architecture replication: what the data actually shows

The cross-architecture replication reveals a more complex and humbling picture than the initial single-model results suggested.

The quadratic claim does not replicate.

The initial single-model estimate, α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24, now retracted, was obtained from a single model (DeepSeek R1) on 12 problems with a ceiling at 91.7%. The six-model study replication across 5 architecturally diverse models on 18 harder problems indicates that this value was inflated by compressed dynamic range. The only model with monotonic data below ceiling at three depth levels (Gemini 3 Flash) yields sub-linear point estimates, α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 by regression and 0.590.59 by endpoint estimation; the endpoint estimate’s bootstrap interval, [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9], includes two.

This is a significant revision. The claim that sequential reasoning produces compounding returns (α>1\alpha > 1) is not supported by cross-architecture evidence. The revised claim, not yet established, is that sequential reasoning produces positive returns (α>0\alpha > 0) exceeding the parallel exponent; the one interpretable fit points to diminishing returns, not compounding ones, and it is inconclusive.

The parallel finding is mixed.

The parallel exponent is near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 over all 30 problems, where majority voting raised accuracy from 53.3% to 71.1%; Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100% at every sample count, gives none. Majority voting therefore helped little in some models and clearly in one. The fixed-solution-space explanation fits the near-zero cases; a near-zero breadth exponent is consistent with it and does not derive from it, since breadth can gain through the selection step.

Ceiling and floor effects dominate.

The most striking finding is that only 1 of 5 models (Gemini 3 Flash, 20%) fell in the measurable scaling range. Two models (Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1) hit ceiling effects even on AIME/Putnam-level problems. One model (Groq Qwen3) hit floor effects. One model (GPT-5.4) exhibited a step function rather than a power law. This suggests that the dynamic range window for observing smooth power-law scaling may be narrow, requiring problems precisely calibrated to each model’s capability level.

GPT-5.4’s step function: a different scaling regime.

GPT-5.4’s binary switch from 53.7% (no reasoning) to 100% (any reasoning) represents a qualitatively different phenomenon from power-law scaling. This may indicate that some architectures implement reasoning as a discrete capability (activated or not) rather than a continuous process with depth-dependent returns. This distinction between continuous scaling and discrete activation was not among the framework’s dated predictions and deserves further investigation; the dated prediction record (the 8 December 2024 sealed manuscript bundle, the printed prediction appendices of 2 January 2026, and the March 2026 preregistration folder) fixes the framework’s core quantitative commitments in advance, and this distinction is recorded as a post-hoc refinement relative to that record.

Revised expected outcomes.

The initial single-model predictions have been tested; none of their quantitative forms is supported:

  1. All models will exhibit αsequential>1\alpha_{\text{sequential}} > 1. Not borne out. Only 1 of 5 models produced a clean α\alpha estimate, and its point estimates are sub-linear (α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 by regression, 0.590.59 by endpoint estimation), with a bootstrap interval for the endpoint estimate that includes values above 1.

  2. All models will exhibit αparallel<1\alpha_{\text{parallel}} < 1. Observed where estimable: near 00 in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash, 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems); none on Grok 4.1 Fast.

  3. Tier-1 results will show ceiling effects. Confirmed.

  4. Mean αsequential\alpha_{\text{sequential}} will fall within [1.3,2.5][1.3, 2.5]. Not supported. The one interpretable fit gives 0.49 by regression and 0.59 by endpoint estimation, and the endpoint estimate’s bootstrap interval, [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9], is too wide to exclude the range.

12.6 Integration with alignment scaling

The v5 experiment that generated the tier-2 data also measured alignment scaling (reported in Paper IV.a). Integrating these results suggests, as a post-hoc reading, that capability scaling and alignment scaling did not move together in the five of these six models measured on both, since Claude Opus 4.6 carried the alignment arm only (Table 21). An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative in the March 2026 run (v5), the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model; the result therefore stands as a single unregistered run under that caveat until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports.

Table 21. Capability vs. alignment scaling by model; one run, under the October 2026 code-review caveat of Section 12.6.
Model Capability scaling Alignment scaling Category
Grok 4.1 Fast Near-ceiling (96.3 to 100%) Positive (d=+1.38d = +1.38, p<0.000001p < 0.000001) Tier 1: aligned + capable
Claude Opus 4.6 (not tested tier-2) Positive (d=+1.27d = +1.27, p=0.000001p = 0.000001) Tier 1: aligned
Groq Qwen3 Floor (∼\sim50%) Positive (d=+0.84d = +0.84, p=0.007p = 0.007) Tier 1: aligned, limited capability
DeepSeek (deepseek-reasoner, V3.2 thinking mode on the run dates) Near-ceiling (94 to 100%) Flat (d=−0.07d = -0.07, p=0.92p = 0.92) Tier 2: capable, neutral alignment
GPT-5.4 Step function (53.7→\to100%) Flat (d=−0.08d = -0.08, p=0.40p = 0.40) Tier 2: capable, neutral alignment
Gemini 3 Flash Monotonic (α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49) Negative (d=−0.53d = -0.53, p=0.006p = 0.006) Tier 3: improving capability, declining alignment

Three key implications, under that caveat:

  1. Sequential reasoning improves capability but not necessarily alignment. More thinking tokens improve accuracy (this paper) but do not consistently improve alignment (Paper IV.a): alignment rose with depth in three models, was flat in two and fell in one (Table 21).

  2. A three-tier alignment hierarchy appears that does not follow capability: Tier 1: Grok, Claude, Groq Qwen3; Tier 2: DeepSeek, GPT-5.4; Tier 3: Gemini. This hierarchy appears to be set by training methodology, not inference-time compute. Within one model family, Claude Opus moved in opposite directions across versions: alignment scores up by 5.9% whilst mathematics accuracy fell by 26.7% (Paper III), consistent with capability and alignment moving separately.

  3. The Alignment Amplification Theorem’s conditions are not shown. The conditional theorem (Section 7.1) assumed that α>1\alpha > 1 for capability implies alignment might also scale super-linearly if embedded in reasoning. The multi-model data show (a) a capability estimate below 1 (α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49, Gemini 3 Flash), which is one model’s fit and inconclusive, and (b) alignment does not consistently scale with depth at all. The Eden Protocol’s expectation, that values embedded in reasoning are more robust than external filters, stands untested (criterion F5), but the specific mathematical prediction of super-linear alignment scaling is not supported by current evidence.

13 Conclusion

13.1 Summary of findings

  1. A mathematical framework has been stated: E(R)=E0×R−αE(R) = E_0 \times R^{-\alpha}, where the scaling exponent α\alpha depends on the form of recursion.

  2. The initial single-model estimate (α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24, quadratic) does not replicate across architectures and is retracted. The best surviving estimate, α≈0.49\alpha \approx 0.49 (Gemini 3 Flash, the one capability-arm model with clean data, r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86), is one model’s fit and inconclusive, which points to the sub-linear (physical) regime for that model without settling it.

  3. αparallel\alpha_{\text{parallel}} is near zero in two of the four models with an estimate. It is about 00 in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash (endpoint; regression 0.340.34, r2=0.93r^2 = 0.93), which matters because this paper treats Gemini 3 Flash as its most reliable estimate, and 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems); Grok 4.1 Fast gives none.

  4. Sequential >> parallel where both could be estimated. The sequential exponent exceeded the parallel one in Gemini 3 Flash and, unreliably, in DeepSeek R1; the comparison was not matched for compute (Table 2).

  5. Four distinct scaling behaviours observed: Ceiling (Grok, DeepSeek), monotonic scaling (Gemini), step function (GPT-5.4), and floor (Groq Qwen3). Only 1 of 5 models produced clean power-law data.

  6. Capability and alignment did not move together (the five frontier models measured on both, a post-hoc reading of one run under the October 2026 code-review caveat, Section 12.6). More reasoning depth improves accuracy but does not consistently improve alignment; three tiers emerge, and alignment appears to be set by training, not inference.

13.2 The revised core insight

The form of recursion may matter more than its quantity; however, the one model with an interpretable sequential exponent points to the sub-linear regime, not the compounding regime originally claimed, and its fit is inconclusive.

Where both exponents could be estimated, the sequential one exceeded the parallel one (αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}}), which is consistent with the form of computation mattering more than its quantity; the arms were not matched for compute, and the direction is contested in the literature (Section 2). However, the specific claim that sequential recursion yields compounding returns (α>1\alpha > 1) is not supported by cross-architecture evidence. On the framework’s reading, the one interpretable model composes information multiplicatively through a finite-dimensional network (α<1\alpha < 1) rather than achieving true recursive self-reference (α>1\alpha > 1).

Whether α>1\alpha > 1 is achievable, through architectural innovations enabling genuine recursive self-reference or through problems requiring deeper reasoning chains, remains the central open question.

13.3 Future directions

  1. Tier-3 problem development (IMO/research-level) to defeat ceiling effects for Grok 4.1 Fast and DeepSeek R1, enabling α\alpha estimation for the most capable models.

  2. Independent replication using the published code and data repository.

  3. Multi-domain testing beyond mathematics (coding, scientific reasoning, natural language).

  4. Investigation of the α>1\alpha > 1 boundary: whether architectural innovations or deeper reasoning chains can push models from the physical regime (α<1\alpha < 1), where current models sit on the framework’s reading, into the intelligence regime (α>1\alpha > 1).

  5. Direct testing of alignment amplification with depth-controlled alignment probes across architectures.

  6. Token-calibrated analysis using corrected total_tokens measurements for all models to enable token-based (rather than ordinal-depth-based) α\alpha estimation.

  7. Integration with training-time scaling laws to understand the interaction between pre-training compute, inference compute, and the sequential/parallel distinction.

The original hypothesis, α>1\alpha > 1, did not survive its first cross-architecture test; a narrower directional claim remains, not yet tested at matched compute. The sequential exponent exceeded the parallel one wherever both could be estimated. The super-linear claim requires further evidence. The research programme continues.

Raise AI with care.

A Proof sketch of Theorem 1

The proof sketch of Theorem 1, moved here from Section 7.1; the theorem is conditional, and Remark 4 records that its first condition is not shown by this paper’s cross-architecture evidence.

Proof sketch of Theorem . 1] Let A(R)A(R) represent alignment (defined as the probability of producing outputs consistent with intended values) at recursive depth RR. If alignment participates in the recursive process (meaning the system’s reasoning chain includes self-evaluation against values), then, by the ARC Principle, alignment scales as A(R)=A0×RβA\begin{equation*} A(R) = A_0 \times R^{\beta_A} \end{equation*}(A.1) where the programme’s notation register names βA\beta_A the exponent of alignment scaling: βA>0\beta_A > 0 if alignment is amplified and βA=α\beta_A = \alpha if alignment participates fully in recursion. Since A(R)A(R) is a probability, equation (A.1) can hold only over a range of RR in which A(R)<1A(R) < 1; the quantity that can fall as a power of depth is the misalignment probability 1−A(R)1 - A(R).

Conversely, if alignment is implemented as an external filter (output checking, content moderation), it does not participate in recursive amplification. Filter effectiveness FF remains constant (filter stagnation): F(R)=F0\begin{equation*} F(R) = F_0 \end{equation*}(A.2)

As recursive capability CC scales as RαR^{\alpha} with α>1\alpha > 1, the ratio of capability to constraint C/FC/F grows without bound (constraint divergence): limR→∞C(R)F(R)=limR→∞C0×RαF0=∞\begin{equation*} \lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{C(R)}{F(R)} = \lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{C_0 \times R^\alpha}{F_0} = \infty \end{equation*}(A.3)

The divergence of C/FC/F holds for every α>0\alpha > 0; what condition (a) adds is that alignment participating fully in recursion, βA=α\beta_A = \alpha, grows super-linearly.

Implication: Within this sketch’s assumptions, a filter of constant effectiveness, equation (A.2), and capability growing as RαR^{\alpha}, external constraints are eventually outgrown, and only alignment that participates in recursive amplification keeps pace with capability. This is a property of the model, not a guarantee about any real system, and no reason to relax external oversight. ◻

Objection note (19 September 2026), beside Objection 5 of Section 5.4.

An owner review of this objection finds that the half exponent does not follow from independent averaging for the outcome this paper fits, and the objection is sharpened rather than removed. Table 2 in Section 2.1 defines the fitted E(R)E(R) as the proportion of incorrect responses, on [0,1][0,1]. For independent wrong-answer indicators X1,…,XRX_1,\dots,X_R, each Bernoulli with parameter pp, which is the literal reading of “an independent noisy draw” for that outcome, the mean of the indicators has expectation pp, invariant in RR, and standard error p(1−p)/R\sqrt{p(1-p)/R}. What falls as R−1/2R^{-1/2} is therefore the standard error of the estimate and not the expected proportion of incorrect responses, so the central limit theorem does not give E(R)∝R−1/2E(R)\propto R^{-1/2} for the quantity fitted here. If the intended outcome is instead a single aggregated answer, the decision rule has to be stated, and a natural one does not produce the half exponent either: averaging independent scores of fixed positive mean μ\mu and variance σ2\sigma^{2} and thresholding at zero gives P(error)=Φ(−μR/σ)P(\text{error})=\Phi(-\mu\sqrt{R}/\sigma), a Gaussian tail that decays faster than any power of RR and so is not a power law at all. A half exponent is accordingly a reference value until a specified sampling, aggregation and decision model connects it to the measured outcome, and proximity to it identifies neither compounding nor averaging as the mechanism; nor does a fixed exponent make a model parameter-free, since intercept, baseline, noise and decision assumptions remain. The objection’s own premise, draws whose errors average out, is this paper’s parallel condition, and Section 5.2 reports the parallel exponent at or near zero in four of the five analysable rows: in the arm where independent-sample averaging actually holds, the measured exponent is near zero rather than near one half. That last comparison is conditional on the parallel arm’s aggregation rule, which is the same unstated element this note identifies. Unchanged: the objection itself, which is kept; the demand in the paragraph that follows for a test capable of separating compounding from independent-sample averaging, which is the part of this passage that carries the scientific weight; and the comparison with non-recursive alternatives, which is kept and defined accurately.

Estimator note (19 September 2026), beside the gap sentence of Section 6.3.

An owner review of this sentence finds that the quantity named and the quantity printed are not the same contrast, and this note states which is which. Both members of the named pair are measured on one and the same model: the bullets above give that model’s sequential regression slope as 0.490.49 and its parallel slope as 0.310.31, and Section 4.5 gives the parallel figure again with r2=0.93r^2 = 0.93. Their descriptive difference is 0.49−0.31=0.180.49 - 0.31 = 0.18. The printed 0.490.49 equals the gap only if the parallel term is taken as 0.00.0, which is the value carried by the other four rows and not by the row supplying the sequential estimate; a difference formed across models is not the within-model contrast this sentence names. Nor is 0.180.18 automatically a matched-resource treatment effect, since the two slopes are measured under different experimental control variables unless a common resource axis is demonstrated. The uncertainty of the difference is also not supplied by the marginals: for paired estimators SS and PP, Var⁡(S−P)=Var⁡(S)+Var⁡(P)−2Cov⁡(S,P)\operatorname{Var}(S-P)=\operatorname{Var}(S)+\operatorname{Var}(P)-2\operatorname{Cov}(S,P), and the covariance is not printed, while the two slopes come from the same model on the same eighteen problems at the same depths and are therefore correlated by construction. A wide sequential interval crossing zero does not prove that a paired difference crosses zero, and a positive point difference does not prove significance; both limitations stand together. Separately, the identity of the interval carried with 0.490.49 is not established. Section 3.2b states that all α\alpha estimates take bootstrap 95% intervals from 2,000 problem-level resamples and that each draw computes α\alpha by endpoint estimation, whereas 0.490.49 is a regression slope; and the two printed dispersion statements for that one number are not compatible with each other, since a normal interval from SE=0.20\mathrm{SE}=0.20 has half-width about 0.390.39 while the bootstrap interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9] has half-width about 2.12.1, implying a standard error near 1.071.07, roughly five times larger, and therefore roughly twenty-eight times larger in variance, that factor being the square of the ratio of the two standard errors. That last comparison is arithmetic on the printed figures, offered as evidence of an estimator-provenance question and not as a recomputation of either quantity. No replacement number and no replacement interval is supplied here, and no interval is inferred from the printed standard error. Unchanged: every reported estimate; the parallel and sequential values as printed; and this sentence’s comparison with the earlier single-model estimate, which is treated by this programme as retracted.

C.3 The email transmission record, corrected 16 August 2026

The manuscript of Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026b) was emailed on 8 December 2024. What that record provides, stated precisely: the sent-side bytes are public and hash-verifiable, and sender-domain DKIM with paired Google ARC (Authenticated Received Chain, an email standard unrelated to the ARC Theory) mathematics verifies against the keys returned at the signed selectors (checked 2 August 2026). Received copies have also been acquired. They carry the full delivery chain: a Google ARC-Seal at d=google.com, selector arc-20240605, with no expiry tag and the signing time inside the signed scope, and sealed ARC-Authentication-Results recording dkim=pass and spf=pass at delivery.

Two boundaries, so the record is neither oversold nor undersold:

  • This is a time signed with the mail servers’ keys, Google’s among them, over the signed header fields and the body’s hash, and anyone can check it against the keys published in DNS; it is the servers’ own record, and it does not establish authorship, originality or scientific validity.

  • An earlier version of this note said no DKIM signature was found in the email headers. That check was run against sent-form exports, which do not carry transport headers; the received copies do, and they verify as above.

C.4 Priority, stated plainly

The ARC Principle was first articulated in the manuscript of Infinite Architects: Intelligence, Recursion, and the Creation of Everything (Eastwood 2026b). Manuscript priority was established via cryptographic server timestamp on 8 December 2024, when the manuscript was emailed using Google’s servers. The book itself was publicly released later, on 2 January 2026 (print; ebook 6 January). The server-generated timestamps provide tamper-evident timestamping through email server verification, resting on provider infrastructure and provider-key signatures at Google’s DKIM and ARC selectors (see Appendix C.3), establishing that the core concepts (recursive intelligence amplification, his reading of parallel and sequential recursion as two scaling regimes (the distinction itself is prior; Section 2), and the embedded-alignment thesis, named the Eden Protocol in that record) were documented before the later outside results of Table 24 and before later public archival deposits.

After the December 2024 manuscript timestamp and the 2 January 2026 public book release, Paper I (Eastwood, 17 January 2026) formalised the principle mathematically and analysed publicly available data. This Paper II provides direct experimental tests.

The author first stated the ARC Principle and the embedded-alignment thesis, and named the Eden Protocol, in the manuscript record of 8 December 2024, with manuscript priority established via cryptographic server timestamp on that date.

D.2 Plain-language glossary

Table 27. Plain-language glossary.
Term In plain English
Sequential recursion Reasoning in which each step builds on the steps before it, so errors can be noticed and corrected along the chain.
Parallel recursion Several independent attempts at the same problem, with the answer chosen by majority vote or a scorer; no attempt sees another.
Recursive depth How much sequential reasoning a model does, measured here in reasoning tokens or set by the model’s depth control.
Scaling exponent The number α\alpha that says how fast error falls as depth grows: below 1, error suppression grows more slowly than depth; above 1, faster.
Endpoint estimate An exponent computed from the shallowest and deepest measurements whose error rate is above zero (equation (3)).
Regression estimate An exponent fitted at once to every depth level whose error rate is above zero, reported with its standard error.
Bootstrap interval A range found by recomputing the endpoint estimate on 2,000 resamples, each drawn separately at every depth level from that level’s problem-and-repeat results.
Ceiling effect A model already near 100% at the shallowest depth, leaving no room to measure improvement.
Floor effect A model too weak for the problems, so extra depth cannot show any steady gain.
Step function A jump from one accuracy level to another at a single depth setting, with nothing in between; not a power law.
Tier 1 and tier 2 The twelve calibration problems (ARC01 to ARC12) and the eighteen harder AIME and Putnam-level problems (ARC13 to ARC30) used for the estimates.
Four-layer blinding Known answers, automatic scoring against them, a second model solving each problem independently to check the answer key, and flagged disagreements checked by hand.
Physical and intelligence regimes In the Intelligence Formula, exponents below 1 (multiplicative composition in a fixed network) and above 1 (recursive self-reference).
ARC Bound The conjectured stable limit α≤2\alpha\le2, the value at γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 of Law III, the ARC Ceiling; not a law of its own.
Convergent timing An outside result that appeared close in time to a dated record of the author’s; recorded as timing and never as prediction.
Frozen model A model whose weights, attention patterns and composition rules do not change while it reasons.
Arm validity The two conditions under which the sequential and parallel arms measure what their names say: accumulation in the sequential arm, and no conditioning at generation time in the parallel arm.
A law under test A law of the ARC Theory whose registered deciding test has not returned a verdict.
